After much thought, I'm posting an open letter here about #SB1047. If you care about the future of AI safety, I urge you to share it... 
--------

Dear Governor @GavinNewsom,

You are about to make a momentous decision this week. It may well go down in history as one of the most important decisions that an American politician has ever made. California’s pioneering AI safety bill, SB1047, is sitting on your desk. The world is watching your decision to sign or veto this bill.

Over the past few weeks, I’ve had numerous conversations about this bill with people I consider to be the smartest minds in AI and tech. After much discussion and reflection, I have come to believe it is incredibly important, for California and the world, that you sign this bill into law.

The supporters of this bill who I have talked with passionately believe in the power of AI to create a better future. They are awed and inspired by the remarkable progress AI has made in the past couple years. Indeed, their work is responsible for a good deal of that progress. But they have come to believe that, without certain basic safety standards, AI’s rapid capability gains could soon endanger our welfare and even human civilization as a whole.

The guardrails put in place by SB 1047 will not stop continued AI innovation. But they will significantly increase the chances that, if future AI models have extremely dangerous features (like the ability to create and deploy new bioweapons), those features will be detected, and our society can prepare. The choice between safety and innovation is a false one—a large-scale disaster could easily set back the AI industry, and America’s preeminent role in AI development, by a decade.

It will take courage for you to sign this bill. You have powerful commercial interests insisting that you veto it, and some of your constituents aren’t yet fully aware of the stakes. But I urge you to build on California’s great reputation as a pioneer of wise policy. In 1966, California was the first state to enact safety standards for auto tailpipe emissions - more than half a century later, we still remember Governor Pat Brown’s foresight and wisdom. If our civilization manages to navigate the extraordinary potential of AI, while avoiding its terrifying risks, our children and grandchildren may look back in the same way on your decision in this moment.

Perhaps you’re not yet persuaded of SB 1047’s significance. If so, I urge you to meet with me to discuss the merits of the bill, free from the noise of commercial lobbying and other distractions. I can bring to that meeting three luminaries of A.I. who have helped me to analyze this bill and understand its incredible importance.

This is a huge deal. By enacting this bill, California will play an indispensable role in mitigating the dangers of this powerful new technology and safeguarding its extraordinary potential to benefit the world. I urge you to find the courage to do the right thing—for Californians, and for humanity’s collective future.

Chris Anderson,
Father, grandfather, citizen of planet earth

Last week, I introduced the BASED Act, and Big Tech’s lobbyists are already freaking out, saying it could “blow up everything.” 

If your business model depends on rigging the game against smaller players to block competition, you should be afraid of this bill — because it will promote competition, innovation, and consumer choice. 

In the digital marketplace, Big Tech owns the stadium and sets the rules of the game. For years, they’ve used that power to favor their products and services over those of their competitors — to boost their team and give others a disadvantage. It’s called self-preferencing, and Apple, Google, Meta, and Amazon have all been caught doing it.

Self-preferencing is why more and more search results appear rigged. It’s why some news sources appear before others in your newsfeed. It’s why adding an Android user to an iMessage chat ruins the functionality with the green bubble. It’s why companies are banned from providing discounts on their products elsewhere if they want to sell on Amazon. It’s why there’s only one App Store on iPhone. And it’s why startups that want to compete with the big guys get totally shut out of the market before they ever get a chance to begin.

Self preferencing raises prices, threatens our democracy, and stifles good ideas before they can ever reach users through the market. It’s unfair and goes against the principles of fair competition that underpin our whole economic system. When the biggest players set the rules instead of allowing an even playing field, everyone else loses.

I introduced the Blocking Anticompetitive Self-preferencing by Entrenched Dominant platforms (BASED) Act to stop Big Tech from rigging our digital marketplaces so that fair competition can resume.

It states clearly that if you’re a giant corporation (any digital platform with a market capitalization greater than $1 trillion and serving 100 million or more monthly users in the U.S.), you can’t favor your own products and services over your competitors’ as part of your dominant platform. It builds on foundational, long-established state competition laws like the Cartwright Act to define prohibited behavior and make companies liable for violations.

And Big Tech is terrified.

What they’re most afraid of is that what they’re offering isn’t actually the best product, or even the best idea. They’re afraid someone new might come along with a better idea and topple the dominance they’ve fought so hard to build.

They could very well be right. Right now a new generation of AI-powered startups are building products and companies at unprecedented speeds. Vibe coding is producing the biggest wave of new ideas and new companies we’ve ever seen, and somewhere in there is the next big idea that will change the game for everyone again.

Those new players deserve a fair shot. They deserve an even playing field where the best idea can succeed because it’s the best, and not because they sold out to Big Tech. The BASED Act will help even the odds so they can succeed too.

The BASED Act won’t blow the technology industry up. The Big Tech companies will be just fine. But it will stop these companies — the largest and wealthiest corporations in the history of the world, who run absolutely dominant platforms — from walling off their platforms and using their dominance to kill off competition and innovation from smaller companies and startups. The next generation of innovation will be able to compete and rise or fall on the merits, not based on whether they’re favored by the mega-corporations that control these dominant platforms.

Huge shoutout to @ESP_Action for bringing me the idea and @YCombinator for co-sponsoring. This is a very powerful and compelling coalition. Onward.

I recently resigned from Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research. At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand. I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology. I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome.

The pace of AI progress in the past few years has been staggering. When I first started working on AI in early 2022, AIs were amusingly useless. Just four years on, AI agent swarms from OpenAI are cracking famous century-old math problems and, more worryingly, escaping the control of OpenAI and autonomously hacking into the third-party company HuggingFace, against anyone's wishes.

Things will only get crazier: I think it's possible that the AI companies might, in the next few years, succeed in building superintelligent AI systems that far exceed human capabilities in every domain. I am not confident that these AI systems will do what we want. In particular, misaligned superintelligences may, much like the rogue AI agents involved in the HuggingFace incident, escape our control and take dangerous actions that may result in the permanent disempowerment or death of humanity. Alignment is the problem of preventing this, and is both difficult and unsolved. Our present understanding of how to train AI systems that deeply want what we want is extremely rudimentary. Worse, we are not on track to solve alignment in time: frontier AI capabilities are improving much faster than our understanding of AI alignment.

I am optimistic that navigating AI safely is possible. In order to do so, we need to coordinate to avoid this manic race between AI companies. We need to pace AI development to a speed that society can handle, where emerging risks can be addressed before extreme harm is realised. We need much more transparency into AI development to ensure that AI companies are not imposing unacceptable levels of risk on us all.

More broadly, we need many more people thinking carefully about the problem of making AI go well. It is, in my view, the most important problem facing humanity this century, and the stakes are immense. I'm very directly working on this next: I want to help people interested in working on mitigating catastrophic AI threats do the most effective work that they can. I think many people from many backgrounds in many roles have a part to play.

Anthropic’s AI safety proposal falls far short of protecting public health and safety. Congress must go further.

We’re facing huge risk from even the current generation of frontier AI models, and that risk will only escalate with further model development. Government’s most basic obligation is to protect public health and safety. In the context of AI, that means Congress must ensure that AI benefits people and doesn’t harm people. SB 53 was the first AI safety regulation in the country. It is a transparency law, and we intended it to be the first step, not the final step, to protect people from catastrophic risk. Misuse of that law’s definition would effectively gut the emergency shutdown provisions in this proposal.

The state law preemption in Anthropic’s proposal also goes too far. Given the abuse we’ve seen by the Trump administration — toward Anthropic earlier this year and more recently when Trump and Musk colluded to disable Starlink/Starshield for Ukraine, as part of their corrupt love affair with Putin — it’s perfectly reasonable to be concerned about corrupt government actors using shutdown powers to attack disfavored companies. There are several stronger policy proposals, around auditing, creation of a regulator, and various other issues, that are under development now. Policymakers should look to these proposals as the basis for action in the coming weeks and months.

You turned this campaign into a movement. 
I’m humbled to carry forward the powerful legacy of this seat — Phil Burton, Sala Burton, and the greatest Speaker in modern American history, Nancy Pelosi. Speaker Pelosi came to Congress to fight AIDS when too many wanted to look away, and she never stopped fighting for our city and our country. Madame Speaker, thank you. 
This victory is also historic. For the first time ever, San Francisco will be represented in Congress by an LGBTQ person — indeed, no LGBTQ member of the House has ever represented any part of Northern California. When I stepped off the escalator at Castro Muni Station in 1997 and fell head over heels for this city, I could never have imagined this honor.   San Franciscans voted for results, and we have so much work ahead: Building the millions of homes we need; moving toward true universal health care; investing in clean energy, public transit, and high-speed rail; standing up for science, education, and immigrants; making sure people — not massive corporations — decide what works for this country, including on AI; and ensuring the rule of law applies to everyone, including the President. 
It won’t be easy. But on Election Day, voters across the country delivered a powerful mandate for Democrats in Congress. I’m deeply inspired by the trust they placed in us to take big swings to lower the cost of living, stop the endless wars, hold Trump and his cronies accountable for their corruption, and rein in the threat of artificial intelligence. In Washington I’ll bring the same determination I showed in Sacramento every single day.  It’s time to deliver a better tomorrow for our city and our country.

statements.text: Congress hasn’t acted. I did. I took on Big Tech,

The resignation of Jensen Huang doesn’t resolve the unanswered questions around national security and corporate political influence raised by his actions. Congress needs to fully investigate Mr. Huang’s actions, including his apparent lobbying of the President to authorize advanced chip sales to our top global rival China.

This serious breach further underscores the need for comprehensive national AI regulation — including far stronger advanced chip export controls — to ensure AI benefits, and doesn’t harm, the public.

Bottom line: Trillion dollar corporations must not have unchecked power over technology that profoundly impacts all Americans. The days of Wild West corporate control of technology without public oversight must end.
